<strong>La loi 21 franchit une nouvelle: Bill 21 has reached a new stage in its tumultuous history: the country’s highest court, the Supreme Court of Canada, has decided to examine its validity. The decision reignites a divisive debate about the place of secularism, minority rights and Quebec identity. Nearly six years after the law was introduced, how do women who wear the headscarf relate to it? La Converse went to meet these women, who continue their fight every day despite the shadow this law casts over their professional and personal futures. Report.
Adoptée en juin 2019, la loi 21 interdit: Adopted in June 2019, Bill 21 prohibits people in positions of authority, including judges, police officers, prison guards and elementary and secondary school teachers, from wearing religious symbols while performing their duties.
Ce choix, que le gouvernement Legault qu: This choice, which the Legault government calls “collective and legitimate,” has nonetheless been repeatedly challenged in court over its consequences for fundamental freedoms. The Supreme Court announced on Thursday, January 23, that it will hear the case, which has already been examined by the Quebec Superior Court in 2021, then by the Court of Appeal last year. While Quebec fiercely defends its right to decide its own laws, the federal government says it is ready to support the challengers before the Supreme Court.
<strong>Une loi qui brime des droits fon: A law that infringes on fundamental rights
<strong>Seattle, jeudi 23 janvier, 6 h d: Seattle, Thursday, January 23, 6 a.m. Zeinab Diab, a doctoral student in social sciences at the Université de Montréal, is glued to her screen. The wait is long and heavy. In a few moments, the Supreme Court of Canada will deliver its decision on the challenge to Bill 21.
Lorsque sa décision favorable à l’examen: When the decision in favour of hearing the challenges finally comes, a mix of relief and hope washes over her. “This is an important moment for the Muslim community, because this law mainly targets women who wear the hijab,” she says.
Selon elle, la loi 21 ne renforce aucune: In her view, Bill 21 does nothing to strengthen secularism in Quebec. “Quebec was already a secular and feminist society. The principles of separation of state and religious institutions, neutrality and freedom of conscience were already respected,” she says.
Mais avec cette loi, poursuit-elle, la l: But with this law, she continues, secularism and women’s rights have been elevated to supreme values, at the expense of other fundamental rights. “Essential freedoms have been suspended: the right to security, to equality, to life. So we have to ask: why override so many rights?” she asks.
Pour Zeinab Diab, la loi 21 réduit la la: For Zeinab Diab, Bill 21 reduces secularism to a question of appearance. “It has been narrowed down to what is visible on bodies, and Muslim women are the ones paying the price,” she says.
Pour protéger la loi contre d’éventuelle: To protect the law from potential legal challenges based on the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the government invoked the notwithstanding clause. This clause allows a law to temporarily override certain protections provided by the Canadian Charter. Bill 21 must therefore be renewed every five years to remain in force.
La loi 21 suspend ainsi l’application de: Bill 21 thus suspends the application of several sections of the Canadian Charter, including those that protect fundamental freedoms and legal rights. The sections concerned are as follows:
<strong>Article 2 :</strong> Garantit le: Section 2: Guarantees fundamental freedoms, including freedom of conscience and religion, freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of association.‍
<strong>Article 15 :</strong> Garantit l: Section 15: Guarantees the right to equality before and under the law and to equal protection of the law, without discrimination, including religious discrimination.
<strong>Une mort sociale : l’effet invis: A social death: the invisible effect of the law
En 2024, Zeinab Diab dépose sa thèse, in: In 2024, Zeinab Diab submitted her thesis, titled Résister à la loi 21 : entre mort sociale et stratégies de survie, praxis musulmane et sororité dans une quête de justice sociale.
Son enquête repose sur les témoignages d: Her research is based on the testimonies of 21 women: 20 teachers – current, former or aspiring – and one lawyer. Through their stories, she brings to light a deep sense of exclusion and incomprehension in the face of a law that targets them directly while denying that they belong to society. “These women are from here, they participate actively in Quebec society. Yet they continue to be perceived as ‘others.’” Contrary to an often-repeated idea, Bill 21 does not target recent immigrants but Quebecers, Zeinab insists: “Half the women in my sample were born here, in Quebec. They are Quebecers, francophones, Montrealers. Yet they face a process of othering in public debate, as if they were never truly ‘from here.’”
Elle qualifie cette expérience de mort s: She describes this experience as social death: a loss of social identity and relationships, an erosion of the sense of belonging. The testimonies she collected also reveal a disconnection from the body. Some women change their appearance so that their hijab isn’t perceived as one. “One woman confided in me: ‘I feel like I’m wearing a costume to go to work. It’s not me anymore,’” Zeinab Diab says.
La mort sociale s’installe peu à peu. «: Social death sets in little by little. “When you barely exist in public space, when your voice isn’t heard, when your rights are violated, you end up feeling invisible,” she concludes.
Portant d’abord sur certaines fonctions: Initially aimed at certain positions of authority, Bill 21 ended up extending to the field of teaching, a sector where women are the majority. For Joe Ortona, chair of the English Montreal School Board (EMSB), the law is a direct obstacle to women’s rights, particularly those of women who wear the hijab.
« En raison de la forte proportion de fe: “Because of the high proportion of women working in Quebec schools, the law has a disproportionate impact on them, particularly on Muslim women who are educated and hold a degree in education, and whose public role has been restricted,” he says. “Bill 21 remains an attempt to solve a problem that doesn’t exist,” he writes in an article published on the EMSB website.
Zeinab est du même avis : « On peut bien: Zeinab agrees: “You can say the law applies to everyone equally, but when you look at the intersection of gender, religion and racialization, you clearly see who bears the brunt of it – it’s gendered Islamophobia.” For her, Bill 21 doesn’t just create barriers to employment; it also restructures the labour market by excluding certain women from the public service.
Face à cette situation, la CSEM a d’aill: In response, the EMSB challenged the law on the basis of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, denouncing discrimination based on sex.
Le mardi 28 janvier au soir, nous recevo: On the evening of Tuesday, January 28, we welcome Idil Issa and Lina El Bakir to the La Converse offices. Both are law students. The two women know each other by name because of their activism, but it’s at La Converse that they truly meet. Very quickly, the conversation comes alive.
Lina El Bakir, 29 ans, termine son stage: Lina El Bakir, 29, is finishing her articling term at the Bar, the last step before she can practise as a lawyer. She wears dangling earrings, discreet under her grey hijab. Across from her, Idil Issa, 40, wears a white and pink turban carefully matched to her jacket and pink sweater. Her resolutely anglophone accent reflects her journey: born in Winnipeg, she spent time in Toronto before settling in Montréal in 2016. Two women, two paths, but the same thirst to contribute to a more just world.
Lina began her law studies in 2016. She dreams of a more inclusive justice system, where racialized people would finally be visible and recognized. But in June 2019, her world collapsed when she received a notification from Radio-Canada: Bill 21 had been adopted. “It was morning. I woke up to that. I was in my third year of law at the University of Ottawa. I saw that notification and I thought, ‘OK, but damn. What’s the point of my studies?’” A feeling of betrayal sets in. The young woman, who cherished Quebec, cannot ignore the rupture taking place within her. “I love Quebec culture, but today, saying that makes me wince. Why should I have to prove my attachment to my province? Why beg to be accepted? If you don’t accept me, too bad. This law has no benefit – not social, not economic, not political. It’s a diversion.”
Ses poings fermés montrent une détermina: Her clenched fists show a new determination: no longer to endure, but to act.
Pour Idil, l’adoption de la loi 21 n’a p: For Idil, the adoption of Bill 21 was not a surprise. After a 10-year career in international communications, she came back to Montréal in 2016, in the middle of the controversy over banning the niqab for people receiving certain public services. A seasoned activist, she founded the group Femmes musulmanes contre le racisme and closely follows political developments in Quebec. “No, it didn’t surprise me,” she begins in a soft voice. “The CAQ had an absolute majority; they didn’t need anyone to pass their laws. It was inevitable.”
C’est en 2021 qu’Idil décide de prendre: In 2021, Idil decided to take a new professional turn. After years of activism, she felt something was missing: “I was fighting for Muslim women’s rights, but I could see it wasn’t enough. My influence remained limited. I needed concrete tools.” She began studying law at McGill, which gave her a certain legitimacy in the public space. “When you’re M<sup>e</sup> Idil, your rights can’t be violated without consequences anymore. You know how to file a complaint, how to navigate the system. It’s another level of power.”
Selon l’étudiante en droit, la loi 21 cr: According to the law student, Bill 21 officially creates two categories of citizens. “It’s simply a law that manufactures structural inequalities and second-class citizens,” she says flatly.
Elle poursuit en exposant une conséquenc: She goes on to describe a very concrete consequence of the law: “Imagine a Quebec school principal who has to hire a teacher. Two candidates have exactly the same qualifications. But the law forces the principal to eliminate the one who wears a religious symbol. It’s not just an unjust law. It’s a law that forces discrimination.”

<strong>Femme, racisée, musulmane : être: Woman, racialized, Muslim: being on every front
« On sait très bien que les lois ont un: “We know very well that laws have normative power,” Lina explains. “Once they’re adopted, they shape mentalities. When Trump introduced his ‘travel ban’ targeting nationals of certain Muslim countries, hate crimes exploded. He was sending a message: ‘It’s okay to be prejudiced against Muslims. They’re all dangerous…’ It’s the same here. Bill 21 implicitly gave the green light. It legitimized the idea that discrimination is acceptable. Overnight, people felt entitled to say about us: ‘Now I have the right to discriminate against you, because the law says it’s okay.’”
<strong><em>Cette pression invisible et: That invisible, heavy pressure we feel every day.
À partir de ce moment, Lina est sur le q: From that moment on, Lina is on alert whenever she goes out: “Imagine, I take the metro and, unconsciously, I scan my surroundings. Who’s around me? Who’s looking at me? Is someone staring? I also ask myself: ‘Am I too close to the edge of the platform? If someone pushes me, will I fall onto the tracks?’”
Elle esquisse un geste, comme si elle se: She makes a gesture as if pressing herself against a wall. “And when I get on the metro, I instinctively stick to the ends of the car.”
« Je fais exactement la même chose ! » p: “I do exactly the same thing!” Idil continues. Why? They answer in unison: “We need to see if there’s danger.”
« Mentalement, l’effet est épuisant, rep: “Mentally, the effect is exhausting,” Lina continues. “At the end of the day, you go home and you’re burned out. And Bill 21 has only reinforced that feeling of being seen as ‘the other.’ It doesn’t matter if you speak French, if you know the culture, if you’ve been here for years… In the eyes of many, you remain a foreigner,” Lina says bitterly.
Depuis 2019, de nombreuses femmes se son: Since 2019, many women have mobilized to denounce what they consider the Islamophobic nature of this law. Today, however, they are more discreet and no longer dare to speak out. According to Idil and Lina, the adoption of Bill 21 has made speaking up difficult, both within the community and on the public stage.
« Il y a des hommes très influents dans: “There are very influential men in the [Muslim] community who are not at all happy with me,” Idil continues. “Because they were the ones who used to represent the Muslim community. Now, it’s the women directly affected who are speaking out, telling their experiences, taking the floor. But how can that be?” she says, furrowing her brows as if imitating them.
« J’essaie d’avoir des discussions avec: “I try to have discussions with them, but if you saw my text messages, they’re not normal conversations: everything is in capital letters, they’re yelling!”
« Peu importe, ce que je sais, c’est que: “Whatever, what I know is that this space belongs to Muslim women. Their voices are the ones that need to be heard. I will never give that up. So yes, I understand why it’s so hard to speak out. There are consequences. And it’s not at all easy.”
Elle jette un regard vers Lina, qui acqu: She glances at Lina, who nods. “And there’s the exhaustion… Since 2019, we’ve been repeating the same things, and nothing changes. Nobody listens to us,” Lina says.
Seulement <strong>0,6 %</strong> du temp: Only 0.6% of speaking time during the public consultations preceding the adoption of Bill 21 was given to teachers who wear the hijab. Yet the word “ headscarf ” came up in 73.8% of the discussions on religious symbols. Source: Modération ou extrémisme ? Regards critiques sur la loi 21
Depuis son bureau à l’Université Laval,: From her office at Université Laval, professor and researcher Khaoula Zoghlami of the Department of Information and Communication speaks with us by videoconference. She goes back over the findings of her study published in the book Modération ou extrémisme ? Regards critiques sur la loi 21, in which she analyzes the speaking time given to Muslim women who wear the headscarf during the Committee on Institutions’ public consultations on Bill 21 in 2019.
« Le chiffre est accablant, souligne-t-e: “The figure is damning,” she says. “0.6% of speaking time was given to the Muslim teachers directly affected by the implementation of this law.” She sets down her coffee cup for a moment, then picks it up again. “To begin with, these women weren’t supposed to be able to testify. Samira Laouni was invited at the last minute, through her organization Communication-Ouverture-Rapprochement Interculturel (C.O.R.), to fill vacant spots after other witnesses withdrew. Idil Issa spoke through the Fédération des femmes du Québec. Bouchra Chelbi was one of four witnesses from the Coalition Inclusion Québec. In other words, they weren’t invited to share their perspective. And it was only after three days of hearings that the only teacher, M<sup>me</sup> Chelbi, was finally able to speak. Before that, many witnesses chosen by the government took turns undermining her credibility, infantilizing her, and even portraying her as dangerous.” She continues, more firmly: “The parliamentary committee wasn’t there to hear them, but to follow a protocol. Nothing more. They were unwelcome in that space.”
Le gouvernement caquiste avait pourtant: The CAQ government had nonetheless repeatedly insisted that Bill 21 targeted no community in particular. But the analysis of parliamentary debates proves otherwise: terms associated with Muslim women’s dress (veil, hijab, headscarf, niqab and burqa) were repeated 296 times, accounting for 73.8% of all the terms used to refer to religious symbols.
Khaoula soupire. « On nous dit que cette: Khaoula sighs. “We’re told that this law doesn’t target any particular category of women or religious minority, but in reality, that’s false. Their headscarf is considered to impair their duties and their ability to act and think. That’s why no one even sees the point of listening to them. The truth is, nobody gives a damn what they think!”
Pour la chercheuse, le « foulard » est d: For the researcher, the “headscarf” has recently become much more than a subject of debate: “It’s become a tug-of-war between the province and Ottawa. A matter of sovereignty. A way for Quebec to assert its independence from the Canadian government. These women are scapegoats.”
Et si la Cour suprême du Canada venait à: And what if the Supreme Court of Canada were to strike down Bill 21? “In Quebec, it wouldn’t be seen as a wrong to be righted, but as federal interference,” she says flatly.
Pour Idil, aucune autre solution que la: For Idil, no solution other than resistance is conceivable. “We have the right to live our lives as we see fit. That’s our social contract. I have the right to choose what’s best for me, just as you have the freedom to make your own choices.” She raises both hands: “They don’t understand. But we won’t give up! Never!”
Lina reconnaît que le combat est loin d’: Lina acknowledges that the fight is far from over. But one thing gives her hope: “Today, more and more young girls who wear the hijab are going into law. They too will take over.” A smile lights up her face. Although she hesitates to continue in the field, aware of the obstacles that await her, she remains proud of those who, fearlessly, will keep moving forward.
Au moment où nous écrivons ces lignes, l: As we write these lines, the date of the hearing on the challenges to Bill 21 is not yet known. In the meantime, the appointment of Robert Leckey to the Quebec Superior Court, announced on January 30, 2025, is generating plenty of reaction. A former dean of McGill’s Faculty of Law, <l1>he has previously spoken publicly about his unease with the law.</l1>
Une annonce qui inquiète notamment Simon: The announcement worries Simon Jolin-Barrette, one of the principal architects of Bill 21, among others, who fears the appointment’s influence on upcoming decisions.
